episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Why is everyone in tech so sad?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [CFJC Today Kamloops] Williams Lake praises work of new Rapid Response Crew and [Williams Lake Tribune] Multiple planned ignitions scheduled for Pear Lake fire near Clinton, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: If AI-powered creative tools relied on unsustainable corporate subsidies are destined to become unaffordable, should rural creators and arts organizations depend on them or invest in durable, community-owned infrastructure instead? Topics include: Sustainability and profitability of AI companies and whether their business models can support long-term tool availability, The difference between disposable digital infrastructure and durable community-based skill transmission, Digital ownership and archival: the importance of local organizations controlling their own creative output rather than relying on free platforms, Worker meaning-making in tech versus tangible satisfaction in trades and hands-on crafts, Rural creative communities' relationship to venture-capital-backed tools versus community-funded workshops.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Chilcotin Partners for Literacy

discussion.central_question: If AI-powered creative tools relied on unsustainable corporate subsidies are destined to become unaffordable, should rural creators and arts organizations depend on them or invest in durable, community-owned infrastructure instead?
discussion.riley_position: Both AI tools and traditional community-based skill-building can coexist as valuable but distinct categories of investment; cheap AI infrastructure is currently useful for solo creators even if it's ultimately disposable, while durable workshop-based work was never meant to run on subscriptions anyway.
riley_key_evidence: Cloud infrastructure, open-weight models, and consumer apps have runway even if OpenAI/Anthropic never turn a profit like normal companies
Historical precedent shows communities adapted when software became unaffordable by adopting open-source alternatives or finding cheaper substitutes
The current subsidy from trillion-dollar companies is better for rural creators right now than the alternative of these tools never existing at all
discussion.casey_position: Rural communities should prioritize building owned, physical archives and community-based skill transmission rather than depending on subsidized AI tools, because the tools represent disposable infrastructure that will inevitably disappear when corporate funding ends, leaving creators worse off than before.
casey_key_evidence: Wells Fargo, Barclays, UBS, and Deutsche Bank independently estimate major tech companies are losing tens of billions annually on AI ventures
Tech workers are hoarding vacation time and refusing to disconnect, signaling industry anxiety about layoffs and corrections rather than confidence
Open-source alternatives to hundred-billion-dollar training runs don't exist in usable form yet, making AI dependency categorically different from swapping photo editors
discussion.resolution: Casey and Riley agreed on a structural split: AI tools are useful but disposable infrastructure, while community workshops and locally-owned archives represent the durable assets that actually survive economic corrections. They united around the concrete recommendation that Cariboo arts organizations should begin archiving their own work on owned hardware immediately, independent of how the AI economics question resolves.
